description: Three humans, zero astronaut experience, unlimited tea. We’re building a game where kids run a Moon or Mars outpost and make the real trade-offs that decide whether a mission succeeds or fails. Power the greenhouse or the radiation shield? Not too simple, not too complex, just fun. Houston, we’re on it.
summary: Horizon Base is a browser-based 3D game for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Students aged roughly 9 to 16 take command of a Moon or Mars outpost. They walk the surface in a spacesuit, scan and collect resources, and build solar panels, batteries, a reactor, greenhouses and radiation shields. They also answer timed radio calls from mission control.
details:
What it does and how it works

Horizon Base is a free 3D browser game for students aged about 12 to 17. The player commands the first outpost at the Moon's south pole (Explorer level) or on Mars (Engineer level). They walk the surface in a spacesuit or plan from above, scan for ice and minerals, and build solar panels, batteries, a nuclear generator, greenhouses, recyclers and radiation shields. Life support, radiation shielding, power and food production compete for the same limited cargo mass, building material and electricity. A reactor solves the polar night but takes cargo space that could have carried crew or food. A greenhouse saves cargo but fails if power drops.

The simulation runs hour by hour on per-person consumption rates, radiation doses, sunlight, resupply windows and events such as dust storms, solar flares and an 8-sol contact blackout on Mars. Decisions arrive as radio calls. Each option shows its effect compared with doing nothing, computed by running the game's own simulation. Each outcome ends with an "In real life" line that names its NASA source. When something fails, the base AI ATLAS explains the cause. At the end, a report card grades five subsystems from A to F, each with a cause sentence.

Benefits and intended impact

Students meet real mission trade-offs because they have to solve them, not read about them. A teacher can run a 40-minute lesson with no setup, and the report card works as a short assessment. A printable teacher guide in Turkish and English is included. The game is in Turkish and English. It is a single HTML file: no server, no account, no cost per user, and it runs offline.

Tools

JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no framework. Three.js (WebGL) for 3D. Web Audio for synthesized sound. All models, icons and textures are generated by code at run time, so there are no image or audio files. Node.js for build and simulation tests, and Playwright with Edge for interface tests. We built it with Claude Code (AI coding agent), as described in the SI field.

Creativity

Prices are computed, not written: every option's effect comes from the game's own simulation. Failures explain themselves with causes taken from that mission's record. Questions appear during repairs and builds, where the fact matters, and a wrong answer has a small, fair cost instead of a game over. The Moon and Mars are two different engineering problems: survive the dark, or become independent of Earth.

What we considered

- Science: values come from published NASA documents. Values that are not real figures are marked in the game, for example the Air Maker output and the lander's nuclear battery.

- Accessibility: a clean screen, plain words and a training mission for beginners.

- Cost: no server and no account, so it is free to run.

- Testing: AI agents played in the roles of a first-time young player and a teacher. We have not yet tested with real students or teachers.
